category: Adjectives used as nouns with the

examples: His uncle got rich selling real estate in Phoenix.

Old newspapers are a rich source of local history.
The chocolate cake was too rich for me to finish.
She makes a rich, creamy sauce for the pasta.
The walls are painted a rich dark red.
He has a rich, warm voice that's perfect for radio.
The rich smell of coffee filled the kitchen.
New Orleans has a rich cultural history.
She's had a long and rich life.
The book gives a richer picture of the war than the movie does.
The valley has rich soil for farming.
Adding compost makes the soil richer.
The hotel lobby was full of rich fabrics and dark wood.
The dining room was decorated in rich velvet and gold.
You're calling me lazy? That's rich, coming from you.
Him complaining about people being late is pretty rich.

senses.head: Having a lot of money or property
examples: His uncle got rich selling real estate in Phoenix.
Tax cuts for the rich are a big issue this election.
They're one of the richest families in the country.

senses.head: rich in: containing or having a large amount of something useful or good
examples: Spinach is rich in iron.
The region is rich in oil and natural gas.
Old newspapers are a rich source of local history.

senses.head: Of food: containing a lot of butter, cream, eggs or sugar, so that a little fills you up
examples: The chocolate cake was too rich for me to finish.
She makes a rich, creamy sauce for the pasta.

senses.head: Of a color, sound or smell: deep, strong and pleasant
examples: The walls are painted a rich dark red.
He has a rich, warm voice that's perfect for radio.
The rich smell of coffee filled the kitchen.

senses.head: Full of interesting variety, detail or meaning
examples: New Orleans has a rich cultural history.
She's had a long and rich life.
The book gives a richer picture of the war than the movie does.

senses.head: Of soil or land: good for growing plants
examples: The valley has rich soil for farming.
Adding compost makes the soil richer.

senses.head: Expensive and beautiful; luxurious
examples: The hotel lobby was full of rich fabrics and dark wood.
The dining room was decorated in rich velvet and gold.

senses.head: That's rich: used informally to say that a criticism is unfair or ridiculous because of who is making it
body: (кто бы говорил; забавно слышать это от тебя)
examples: You're calling me lazy? That's rich, coming from you.
Him complaining about people being late is pretty rich.

entries.position: both — also with the for rich people as a group: the rich are; the ironic That's rich sense goes only after a verb
entries.takes: in + noun (having a lot of something: rich in iron)
entries.contrast: The rich means rich people as a group and always takes a plural verb: The rich are getting richer, not The rich is. It never takes a plural -s: the riches is a different word, a noun meaning great wealth. For one person say a rich man, a rich woman or a rich person, never a rich. Russian богатый чем-то is rich in, not rich of: rich in oil. About food, rich means full of butter, cream or sugar and can be praise; Russian жирный is fatty or greasy, which sound negative. That's rich! is ironic: the critic is guilty of the same thing. Wealthy is the more formal, more polite word, and only for money.

examples: She was very young when she became mayor.
The coach wants a younger team next season.
My younger sister lives in Denver.
They have two young kids, ages three and five.
When I was young, we spent every summer at the lake.
The show isn't suitable for young children.
It's still a young company, only three years old.
Come on, the night is still young!
My grandmother is eighty but very young at heart.
You look younger with short hair.
That dress is a little young for her.

senses.head: Having lived or existed for only a short time; not old
examples: She was very young when she became mayor.
The coach wants a younger team next season.
My younger sister lives in Denver.

senses.head: Being a child; not yet grown up
examples: They have two young kids, ages three and five.
When I was young, we spent every summer at the lake.
The show isn't suitable for young children.

senses.head: In an early stage; recently started or formed
examples: It's still a young company, only three years old.
Come on, the night is still young!

senses.head: Looking, feeling or acting like a young person, or meant for young people
examples: My grandmother is eighty but very young at heart.
You look younger with short hair.
That dress is a little young for her.

entries.position: both — also with the for young people as a group: the young
entries.comparison: -er/-est — younger, youngest, both said with a hard g: /ˈjʌŋɡər/, /ˈjʌŋɡɪst/
entries.contrast: The young means young people as a group and takes a plural verb: The young are often the first to try new apps. For one person say a young man, a young woman or a young person, never a young. Its young (a bird feeding its young) is a different use: a noun meaning an animal's babies. The comparative and superlative add a /ɡ/ the base word doesn't have: young /jʌŋ/ but younger /ˈjʌŋɡər/. Russian младший брат is my younger brother (or little brother), and младший сын among three or more is the youngest son; junior is for rank, not family. About children, young often means small: young children are маленькие дети, not teenagers.

entries.meaning: Having no home, and usually living on the street, in a car or in a shelter. ---
examples: A homeless man was sleeping in the doorway.
The shelter serves hot meals to the homeless every night.
After the fire, forty families were homeless.
entries.position: both — also with the for homeless people as a group: the homeless
entries.contrast: The homeless takes a plural verb: The homeless need more than a bed for the night. It never takes -s, and one person is a homeless man, a homeless woman or a homeless person, never a homeless. Many American writers and charities now prefer homeless people or people experiencing homelessness, because the homeless can sound as if people were only a category. The noun for the problem is homelessness: Homelessness is rising, not Homeless is rising. Don't confuse it with homesick (missing home) or homely, which in American English means plain or unattractive.

entries.meaning: Without a paid job, especially when you want one. ---
examples: He's been unemployed since the plant closed.
The program helps the long-term unemployed find training.
Unemployed workers can apply for benefits online.
entries.position: both — also with the for people without jobs as a group: the unemployed
entries.comparison: not gradable — but long-term unemployed is common
entries.contrast: The unemployed takes a plural verb (The unemployed are) and never takes -s; one person is an unemployed worker or someone who is unemployed, never an unemployed. The noun for the situation is unemployment: Unemployment is at 4 percent, not Unemployed is. Russian он безработный is an adjective after a verb in English: He's unemployed. In everyday speech Americans often say out of work or between jobs; jobless is common in news headlines.

examples: Two injured passengers were taken to the hospital.
The injured were treated at the scene.
Our best player is injured and will miss the game.
Behind his jokes there was a lot of injured pride.
She spoke in an injured tone, as if we had betrayed her.
The injured party can sue for damages.
The contract lets the injured party cancel the deal.

senses.head: Physically hurt, for example in an accident, a fall or a game
examples: Two injured passengers were taken to the hospital.
The injured were treated at the scene.
Our best player is injured and will miss the game.

senses.head: Of feelings: offended or upset because you have been treated unfairly
examples: Behind his jokes there was a lot of injured pride.
She spoke in an injured tone, as if we had betrayed her.

senses.head: In law: harmed or treated wrongly by someone else's actions
examples: The injured party can sue for damages.
The contract lets the injured party cancel the deal.

entries.position: both — also with the for injured people as a group: the injured; the 'offended' and legal senses go mostly before a noun: injured pride, the injured party
entries.comparison: not gradable — say badly, seriously or slightly injured
entries.contrast: The injured means the people who were hurt and takes a plural verb: The injured were taken to three hospitals. For one person say an injured man or one of the injured, never an injured. English splits Russian раненый, травмированный, пострадавший by cause: injured is hurt in an accident, a fall or a game (an injured player); wounded is hurt by a weapon (wounded soldiers); hurt is the everyday word, mostly after a verb (Was anyone hurt?). Things are damaged, not injured: a damaged car. He was injured in a crash is usually the passive of the verb injure.

examples: Her grandfather went blind in his seventies.
He's been blind in one eye since the accident.
The museum offers tours for the blind with objects you can touch.
Parents are often blind to their own kids' faults.
The company seemed blind to the risks.
No one was more blind to the problem than the boss himself.
The soldiers followed orders with blind obedience.
He stormed out in a blind rage.
It takes blind faith to invest in a company like that.
In a blind taste test, most people picked the cheaper cola.
My friends set me up on a blind date.
The judges do a blind review, so they never see the writers' names.
Slow down, there's a blind curve ahead.
The motorcycle was right in my blind spot.
The back of the warehouse is a blind wall with no windows.
Every idea we tried led us up a blind alley.

senses.head: Unable to see, from birth or because of illness or injury
examples: Her grandfather went blind in his seventies.
He's been blind in one eye since the accident.
The museum offers tours for the blind with objects you can touch.

senses.head: blind to: not noticing, or not wanting to accept, something such as a fault or a danger
examples: Parents are often blind to their own kids' faults.
The company seemed blind to the risks.
No one was more blind to the problem than the boss himself.

senses.head: Not based on reason or careful thought; too strong to control
examples: The soldiers followed orders with blind obedience.
He stormed out in a blind rage.
It takes blind faith to invest in a company like that.

senses.head: Done without seeing or knowing something important in advance
examples: In a blind taste test, most people picked the cheaper cola.
My friends set me up on a blind date.
The judges do a blind review, so they never see the writers' names.

senses.head: Hard or impossible to see around or past, so you can't see what is coming
examples: Slow down, there's a blind curve ahead.
The motorcycle was right in my blind spot.

senses.head: Of a wall, an alley or a passage: having no opening or no way through
examples: The back of the warehouse is a blind wall with no windows.
Every idea we tried led us up a blind alley.

entries.position: both — also with the for blind people as a group: the blind; the 'without judgment', 'without seeing', 'hard to see around' and 'no opening' senses go only before a noun: blind faith, a blind curve
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — blinder, blindest, more blind; rare in the sight sense, where English says partially, completely or legally blind
entries.takes: to + noun (not noticing: blind to the risks); in + one eye (blind in one eye)
entries.contrast: The blind means blind people as a group and takes a plural verb: The blind are, a school for the blind. One person is a blind man, a blind woman or a blind person, never a blind; many people prefer blind people or people who are blind, and visually impaired includes people with some sight. The noun blind is a window covering: Pull down the blinds. Losing your sight is go blind. Russian вслепую after a verb is usually without looking or blindly (He signed the papers without reading them), but set phrases keep the adjective: a blind date, a blind taste test. A street with no way out is a dead end; a blind alley is mostly figurative.

examples: She's deaf in her left ear.
Grandpa is getting deafer every year, so speak up.
The theater has captioned shows for the deaf.
The city council was deaf to the neighbors' complaints.
Our warnings fell on deaf ears.
He turned a deaf ear to all our advice.
Deaf culture has its own theater, poetry and humor.
She grew up in a Deaf family where everyone signed.

senses.head: Unable to hear, completely or partly
examples: She's deaf in her left ear.
Grandpa is getting deafer every year, so speak up.
The theater has captioned shows for the deaf.

senses.head: deaf to: unwilling to listen to or pay attention to something
examples: The city council was deaf to the neighbors' complaints.
Our warnings fell on deaf ears.
He turned a deaf ear to all our advice.

senses.head: Deaf: belonging to the community of deaf people who share sign language and a culture
examples: Deaf culture has its own theater, poetry and humor.
She grew up in a Deaf family where everyone signed.

entries.position: both — also with the for deaf people as a group: the deaf
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — deafer, deafest, more deaf; in the hearing sense English usually says partially, profoundly or completely deaf
entries.takes: to + noun (refusing to listen: deaf to our complaints); in + one ear (deaf in one ear)
entries.contrast: Deaf is /dɛf/, rhyming with chef, not /diːf/. The deaf takes a plural verb (a school for the deaf), and one person is a deaf man or a deaf person, never a deaf. With a capital, Deaf names the community and culture of people who use sign language; deaf and dumb and deaf-mute are offensive. For partial hearing loss Americans say hard of hearing. Russian глухой has meanings deaf doesn't: a remote place is remote (a remote village, not a deaf village), a muffled sound is dull or muffled (a dull thud), a wall with no windows is blank, and thick forest is dense.

examples: The law protects disabled workers from discrimination.
Her son has been disabled since a car accident.
The new buses make it easier for the disabled to get around town.
You need a disabled parking placard to park there.
All the disabled parking spots near the entrance were taken.
A disabled truck is blocking the left lane.
Cookies are disabled in your browser.

senses.head: Having a physical or mental condition that limits how a person moves, senses things or does everyday activities
examples: The law protects disabled workers from discrimination.
Her son has been disabled since a car accident.
The new buses make it easier for the disabled to get around town.

senses.head: Meant for use by people with disabilities
examples: You need a disabled parking placard to park there.
All the disabled parking spots near the entrance were taken.

senses.head: Of a machine, a vehicle or a feature: not working, or switched off
examples: A disabled truck is blocking the left lane.
Cookies are disabled in your browser.

entries.position: both — also with the for disabled people as a group: the disabled; the 'for people with disabilities' sense goes only before a noun: disabled parking
entries.comparison: not gradable — say severely, partially or permanently disabled
entries.form: -ed participle of disable, from dis- + able
entries.contrast: Russian инвалид is not English invalid: for a person that word is old-fashioned and offensive, and pronounced /ɪnˈvælɪd/ it means 'not valid' (an invalid password). Say a disabled person or a person with a disability; handicapped sounds dated in the US. The disabled takes a plural verb and never takes -s; one person is never a disabled, and many Americans prefer disabled people or people with disabilities. On US signs, parking spaces and restrooms are usually accessible or handicapped. A disabled car or phone setting is broken or switched off, which has nothing to do with people.

examples: She comes from a wealthy family in Connecticut.
Tax breaks for the wealthy are unpopular with voters.
It's one of the wealthiest suburbs in the country.
Wyoming is wealthy in coal and natural gas.
The country is wealthy in natural resources but has few good roads.

senses.head: Having a lot of money, property or valuable things
examples: She comes from a wealthy family in Connecticut.
Tax breaks for the wealthy are unpopular with voters.
It's one of the wealthiest suburbs in the country.

senses.head: wealthy in: having a large amount of a natural resource or other valuable thing
examples: Wyoming is wealthy in coal and natural gas.
The country is wealthy in natural resources but has few good roads.

entries.position: both — also with the for wealthy people as a group: the wealthy
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — wealthier, wealthiest, more wealthy
entries.contrast: The wealthy takes a plural verb (The wealthy are moving out of the city) and never takes -s; one person is a wealthy man or a wealthy woman, never a wealthy. Wealthy is more formal and more polite than rich, and it covers only money and resources: food, colors and voices are rich, never wealthy (a rich chocolate cake). The comparative changes y to i: wealthier, wealthiest.

examples: The program offers free tutoring to disadvantaged kids.
Schools in the most disadvantaged neighborhoods got extra funding.
The grants go first to the disadvantaged.
Small farmers feel disadvantaged next to the big agricultural companies.
Students without internet at home were more disadvantaged than anyone when classes moved online.

senses.head: Lacking the money, education or opportunities that most people in a society have
examples: The program offers free tutoring to disadvantaged kids.
Schools in the most disadvantaged neighborhoods got extra funding.
The grants go first to the disadvantaged.

senses.head: In a worse position than other people in a particular situation
examples: Small farmers feel disadvantaged next to the big agricultural companies.
Students without internet at home were more disadvantaged than anyone when classes moved online.

entries.русский: малообеспеченный, социально незащищённый; в невыгодном положении
entries.position: both — also with the for disadvantaged people as a group: the disadvantaged
entries.form: dis- + advantaged, from the noun advantage
entries.contrast: The disadvantaged takes a plural verb and never takes -s; one person is a disadvantaged student or someone from a disadvantaged background, never a disadvantaged. It is a polite, official word for poor, used about groups, schools and neighborhoods more than about one person you know. For a single situation the everyday phrase is at a disadvantage (Short players are at a disadvantage), and disadvantaged by + noun is usually the passive of the verb disadvantage. Russian неблагополучный is often better as troubled (a troubled family) when the problem is not money.

entries.meaning: Charged with a crime or said to have done something wrong, but not yet proved guilty. ---
examples: The accused man said nothing during the hearing.
The accused was led into the courtroom in handcuffs.
Police have released the name of the accused shooter.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive of accuse (She was accused of fraud); also with the for the person or people on trial: the accused
entries.contrast: Unlike the rich or the young, the accused often means one person, so the verb follows the meaning: The accused was found guilty (one defendant), The accused were all released (several). It never takes -s. Don't confuse it with accusing, which describes the one doing the blaming: an accusing look is обвиняющий взгляд, while the accused man is обвиняемый. Accused of + noun or -ing belongs to the verb: He is accused of stealing. In US news, accused before a noun stresses that nothing is proved yet: the accused gunman.

examples: The form asks whether your parents are living or deceased.
The house was divided among the deceased man's children.
The family of the deceased has asked for privacy.
entries.position: both — also with the for a dead person or dead people: the deceased
entries.form: -ed participle of the old verb decease
entries.contrast: Deceased is formal and legal; in everyday speech say dead, or late before a name or a family word: her late husband (её покойный муж). Unlike the rich or the young, the deceased usually means one particular dead person and then takes a singular verb: The deceased was a retired teacher; for several people the verb is plural. It never takes -s. Don't confuse it with diseased /dɪˈziːzd/, 'sick, affected by a disease' (diseased trees): deceased has an /s/ sound, /dɪˈsiːst/.

examples: The church collects coats for needy families every winter.
The scholarship goes to the neediest students first.
Volunteers serve Thanksgiving dinner to the needy.
Her new boyfriend is really needy; he texts her every hour.
Our puppy got even needier after we moved.
I don't want to seem needy, but can you call me when you land?

senses.head: Poor; not having enough money, food or other basic things
examples: The church collects coats for needy families every winter.
The scholarship goes to the neediest students first.
Volunteers serve Thanksgiving dinner to the needy.

senses.head: Wanting too much attention, love or reassurance from other people
examples: Her new boyfriend is really needy; he texts her every hour.
Our puppy got even needier after we moved.
I don't want to seem needy, but can you call me when you land?

entries.position: both — also with the for poor people as a group: the needy
entries.comparison: -er/-est or more/most — needier, neediest, more needy
entries.contrast: The needy takes a plural verb and never takes -s: The needy are; one person is a person in need or part of a needy family, never a needy. In the money sense needy sounds a little old-fashioned, and people in need or low-income families are common today. In informal American English needy more often describes someone who wants too much attention, and it is a criticism: He's so needy. It doesn't mean нужный: something you need is necessary or needed.

examples: He grew up in a privileged family on the Upper East Side.
College was easier for the privileged than for the rest of us.
She knows she's more privileged than most of her students.
I'm privileged to be here tonight.
We were privileged to see the whales up close.
What you tell your lawyer is privileged.
The memo contained privileged information.
Only privileged accounts can change these settings.
A few privileged guests got to go backstage.

senses.head: Having advantages, money or opportunities that most people do not have
examples: He grew up in a privileged family on the Upper East Side.
College was easier for the privileged than for the rest of us.
She knows she's more privileged than most of her students.

senses.head: Honored and lucky to have a particular experience
examples: I'm privileged to be here tonight.
We were privileged to see the whales up close.

senses.head: Of information or communication: protected by law from being shared or used in court
examples: What you tell your lawyer is privileged.
The memo contained privileged information.

senses.head: Having special rights or access that ordinary users or members do not have
examples: Only privileged accounts can change these settings.
A few privileged guests got to go backstage.

entries.position: both — also with the for privileged people as a group: the privileged; the 'honored' sense goes only after a verb: I'm privileged to
entries.contrast: The privileged takes a plural verb and never takes -s; one person is a privileged kid or someone from a privileged background, never a privileged. In American talk about race, class and money, privileged is often a criticism: You're privileged and you don't see it. But privileged to + verb is modest and polite: I feel privileged to work here means 'I'm honored', close to для меня большая честь. Privileged information is protected by law, not just secret. It is said in three syllables or two, /ˈprɪvəlɪdʒd/ or /ˈprɪvlɪdʒd/, and the ending is /ɪdʒd/, never /aɪdʒd/.

entries.meaning: Poor, and without the education, health care or opportunities that most people have. ---
examples: The camp is free for kids from the city's most underprivileged neighborhoods.
She raises money for the underprivileged in her city.
Most of the families in the district are underprivileged.
entries.position: both — also with the for poor people as a group: the underprivileged
entries.contrast: The underprivileged takes a plural verb and never takes -s; one person is an underprivileged child, never an underprivileged. Despite privilege inside it, it is not about legal rights: it means poor and without the chances others have, close to disadvantaged. Russian бесправный is without rights or powerless. It is a slightly old-fashioned, official word; American nonprofits now often say low-income instead.

examples: The cause of the fire is still unknown.
He left the company for unknown reasons.
An unknown number of people were still inside.
The movie turned an unknown actress into a star.
The band was unknown outside Seattle until 1991.
Unknown to his wife, he had borrowed money against the house.
The word was unknown to most of the class.
It was a disease unknown to doctors fifty years ago.

senses.head: Not known; not identified or not yet discovered
examples: The cause of the fire is still unknown.
He left the company for unknown reasons.
An unknown number of people were still inside.

senses.head: Not famous; not known to the public
examples: The movie turned an unknown actress into a star.
The band was unknown outside Seattle until 1991.

senses.head: unknown to someone: not known by that person, or happening without their knowledge
examples: Unknown to his wife, he had borrowed money against the house.
The word was unknown to most of the class.
It was a disease unknown to doctors fifty years ago.

entries.position: both — also after a noun with to: a man unknown to the police; the unknown is a singular abstract noun, not a group of people
entries.comparison: not gradable — strengthen with completely, largely or relatively; for 'less famous' say less known or lesser-known
entries.takes: to + person (not known by: unknown to most voters)
entries.contrast: Unlike the rich or the young, the unknown is not a group of people: it means everything that is not known and takes a singular verb. Fear of the unknown is страх перед неизвестностью. For people you don't know, add a noun: an unknown caller, unknown attackers. Unknown to me at the start of a sentence means 'without my knowing', like без моего ведома: Unknown to her parents, she had quit school. As a countable noun, an unknown is a person who isn't famous (a total unknown) or a fact nobody knows yet (too many unknowns); those are nouns.

examples: Medics carried the wounded soldiers to the helicopter.
The wounded were taken to a field hospital.
A wounded deer ran into the woods.
She gave him a wounded look and left the room.
After the breakup he felt wounded and embarrassed.
It was just wounded pride, nothing more.

senses.head: Hurt by a weapon such as a gun, a knife or a bomb
examples: Medics carried the wounded soldiers to the helicopter.
The wounded were taken to a field hospital.
A wounded deer ran into the woods.

senses.head: Emotionally hurt or offended
examples: She gave him a wounded look and left the room.
After the breakup he felt wounded and embarrassed.
It was just wounded pride, nothing more.

entries.position: both — also with the for wounded people as a group: the wounded
entries.comparison: not gradable — say badly, seriously or mortally wounded
entries.form: -ed participle of the verb wound, from the noun wound (an injury)
entries.contrast: The wounded takes a plural verb (The wounded were flown to Germany) and never takes -s; one person is a wounded soldier or one of the wounded, never a wounded. Wounded is for injuries from a weapon (a gun, a knife, a bomb), especially in war or crime; someone hurt in a car crash or a game is injured. Wound the injury and wounded have /uː/: /ˈwuːndɪd/. Wound with /aʊ/ is the past tense of wind (She wound the clock) and has nothing to do with this word.
